stories.headline: Appeals court lets Army detonate degraded explosives in Iowa on Wednesday
stories.summary: A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block the Army from detonating several tons of degraded lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa. The Army said it will carry out the detonation on Wednesday, after a day in which President Trump said the plan depended on the court and on Iowa's incoming Democratic governor.
stories.why_it_matters: Lead azide contains lead, and residents and environmental groups have raised concerns about contamination and health risks from the blast; the Army says the material is unstable and has to be removed.
stories.background: The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown holds about five tons of lead azide, a chemical used in bomb-making that has degraded in storage. The Army planned to destroy it in controlled detonations last week under an emergency permit from the Environmental Protection Agency. Environmental groups sued in the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to stop it, and the plan was paused. Iowa is between governors: Republican Kim Reynolds is leaving office and Democrat Rob Sand was elected this month to succeed her.

Environmental groups had asked the 8th Circuit to halt the detonation, challenging the EPA's emergency permit, according to Earthjustice.

stories.headline: Lawmakers in both parties object to Trump's role in Nvidia CEO's reinstatement
stories.summary: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, 11 days after he resigned over an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and President Trump said he had 'convinced' the company to do it. Republicans and Democrats in Congress criticized the intervention and plan to question Huang. The same day, the Commerce Department put Megaspeed, the company at the center of the scandal, on a trade blacklist.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the stock market, so its swings show up in many retirement accounts, and the episode raises questions about how far a president should go in pressing a private company's board and about the security of advanced AI chips.
stories.background: Jensen Huang founded Nvidia, whose chips power most artificial intelligence systems. He resigned earlier this month after an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a former executive of the Singapore-based AI firm Megaspeed who is suspected of spying for China, became public; Megaspeed has been accused of funneling AI chips to China. Last week Nvidia's board chair told investors the board did not intend to bring him back. Trump publicly pressed for his return, and on Monday the board reversed itself.

stories.headline: Court unseals redacted records from federal search of Rep. Ilhan Omar's home
stories.summary: A federal court on Monday released heavily redacted records about the Oct. 12 search of Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington home, after prosecutors made a late attempt to stop the release. The filings show the investigation reaches back decades and that the government and a magistrate judge argued over the constitutional protections owed to a sitting member of Congress.
stories.why_it_matters: Searches of a sitting lawmaker's home are rare, and the records give the public its first look at how a court weighed a criminal investigation against the Constitution's protections for members of Congress.
stories.background: Omar is a Democratic congresswoman from Minnesota and a frequent target of criticism from President Trump. Homeland Security Investigations agents searched her Washington home on Oct. 12 and took her phone, computers and passport. The warrant and related filings were sealed until news organizations and others asked for them to be made public. Last week Chief Judge James Boasberg said most of the 67-page warrant affidavit should stay sealed for now but that the legal arguments over lawmakers' protections should be released. Omar has denied wrongdoing.

stories.headline: Trump, in Justice Department speech, criticizes Newsom's death row commutations and vows faster federal executions
stories.summary: President Trump used a speech at Justice Department headquarters on Monday to condemn California Gov. Gavin Newsom's decision to commute the death sentences of 548 prisoners, and said he would sign an order to speed up capital punishment at the federal level. Newsom the same day called for limits on the presidential pardon power.
stories.why_it_matters: The exchange puts the death penalty and clemency powers at the center of national politics, and an order to expedite federal executions would directly affect people on federal death row and victims' families waiting on those cases.
stories.background: Newsom, a Democrat seen as a possible 2028 presidential candidate, announced earlier this month that he would convert the sentences of everyone on California's death row to life in prison without parole. California has not carried out executions under a moratorium Newsom imposed in 2019. Trump has pushed to expand use of the federal death penalty since returning to office. Presidents rarely give speeches at the Justice Department, which is meant to operate at some distance from the White House.

stories.summary: The 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Monday that a federal judge erred when he found President Trump had waited too long to raise an immunity defense in his New York hush money case. stories.background: ICE is the federal agency that arrests and deports people who are in the country without legal status. stories.headline: Ukraine says it sank a Russian warship in Libya as the war spreads beyond the front
stories.summary: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was behind naval drone attacks that sank a Russian warship and damaged a sanctioned cargo vessel in Libya, thousands of miles from the front line. Ukraine called the strikes lawful self-defense. Zelenskyy has also confirmed a drone strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland, while Poland reported a Russian drone in its airspace days after Russian missiles landed on its territory.
stories.why_it_matters: The fighting between Russia and Ukraine is now reaching the Mediterranean, the Baltic and NATO territory, which raises the chance of other countries being drawn in and of disruption to shipping routes.
stories.background: Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and the war is now in its fifth year. Ukraine has used explosive-laden sea drones to hit Russian ships in the Black Sea, and reporting earlier this year said Ukrainian forces were operating in Libya and had attacked a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean. Libya is split between rival administrations in Tripoli in the west and in the east, where Russia has a military presence and where Benghazi is located. Russia continues nightly air attacks on Ukrainian cities.

stories.headline: COP31 climate summit ends without a deal after split over fossil fuels
stories.summary: The United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, ended without an agreement after the European Union and other parties refused to accept a final text that lacked language on phasing out fossil fuels. The EU now plans to seek changes to how the UN talks are run, the Financial Times reported.
stories.why_it_matters: These yearly talks are where governments set shared goals for cutting emissions and paying for climate damage; a failed summit means no new global commitments this year, and experts quoted by the AP say poorer countries could be hit hardest.
stories.background: COP is the annual UN conference where nearly every country negotiates climate action, and decisions require consensus. This year's meeting, COP31, was held in Antalya, Turkey. An early draft called for faster action to phase out fossil fuels, but a later, shorter draft removed that language as the deadline approached. Countries were also divided over climate finance, the money richer nations provide to help poorer ones cut emissions and cope with climate impacts.

stories.summary: Wall Street posted its biggest one-day rally since April 2025 on Monday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's chief executive, reversing part of last week's sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks. By Tuesday morning the move was fading: Nasdaq futures pointed to a drop of about 2%, with Nvidia and Anthropic lower in premarket trading.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia and other AI companies make up a large share of the stock indexes that most retirement accounts and index funds track, so swings this large show up directly in people's savings. Analysts quoted in today's coverage disagree on whether the turbulence is over.
stories.background: Nvidia makes the chips that power most artificial intelligence systems and is one of the most valuable companies in the world. Jensen Huang, its co-founder, resigned as chief executive on Nov. 12 and the board named finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO; the company's announcement gave no reason, and news reports tied the departure to an affair and a related spying investigation. On Nov. 17 the board's chairman said it did not intend to bring him back. Stocks tied to AI then sold off sharply late last week. News of Huang's reinstatement followed, and markets rebounded on Monday.

On Tuesday morning Nasdaq futures pointed to a decline of about 2%, and Nvidia and Anthropic shares fell in premarket trading, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Reuters reported that U.S. stock futures and European shares slipped as chip stocks cooled after the Nvidia-led rally.

RBC Capital Markets derivatives strategist Amy Wu Silverman told Bloomberg the VIX volatility index was "still pretty inflated" after the surge in Nvidia shares.

stories.headline: CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler in a $44 billion all-stock deal
stories.summary: Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike agreed on Monday to acquire rival Zscaler in a deal valued at about $44 billion, combining two of the industry's largest firms. CrowdStrike chief executive George Kurtz defended the purchase in a CNBC interview. The companies said the deal needs regulatory approval.
stories.why_it_matters: Many employers, banks, hospitals and government agencies rely on these two companies to protect their networks, so the merger concentrates a large part of that work in one vendor. For shareholders, it is one of the year's largest technology deals.
stories.background: CrowdStrike sells software that protects computers and servers from hacking; Zscaler secures the connections between workers and the applications they use, an approach known as zero trust. Both are based in the United States and sell mainly to large organizations. The New York Times reported that the deal comes as companies and governments worry about hacks made easier by advances in artificial intelligence. CrowdStrike reported quarterly results on the same day it announced the deal.

facts.text: CrowdStrike agreed to acquire Zscaler in a deal valued at about $44 billion that would create a cybersecurity giant, the Associated Press reported.

The deal is all stock: Zscaler shareholders would receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each Zscaler share, about a 34% premium to Zscaler's Nov. 20 closing price, according to the companies' announcement filed with the SEC.
The companies said existing CrowdStrike shareholders would own about 84.1% of the combined company, and that closing is subject to regulatory approvals.
CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz defended the acquisition on CNBC, calling it a "winning combination".
The New York Times reported the deal comes amid worries among companies and governments about AI-enabled hacking.

framing.note: Emphasizes scale: a deal that would "create a cybersecurity giant".
Calls it two major firms that will "combine", and its summary ties the deal to AI-driven hacking fears.
The CEO "defends" the deal, implying investor doubts.

stories.headline: Sanofi agrees to buy U.S. biotech Insmed for $41 billion
stories.summary: French drugmaker Sanofi agreed on Tuesday to buy U.S. biotechnology company Insmed for $41 billion, the largest deal in the drug industry in about three years. Insmed shares rose 14% on the news, CNBC reported.
stories.why_it_matters: Large drugmakers buy smaller ones to replace income from medicines that are about to face cheaper generic competition, which shapes which new drugs get funded and sold. In the digest, the deal was covered by center and left-leaning business outlets only.
stories.background: Sanofi is one of the world's largest pharmaceutical companies, and its top-selling drugs are due to lose patent protection toward the end of the decade, which would let generic makers compete and cut its revenue. Insmed is a U.S. biotech whose main product is the lung drug Brinsupri. Bloomberg reported on Nov. 19 that Sanofi was weighing a takeover, and Insmed's shares jumped on that report. The agreement announced Tuesday confirms the deal.

facts.text: Sanofi agreed on Tuesday to pay $41 billion for Insmed.
Insmed shares rose 14% after the announcement, CNBC reported.
MarketWatch called it the biggest biotech deal in nearly three years; CNBC called it the pharmaceutical industry's biggest in three years.
Both outlets said the purchase is meant to help offset revenue Sanofi stands to lose as key drugs lose exclusivity later this decade.
Bloomberg first reported on Nov. 19 that Sanofi was considering a bid, with Insmed's lung drug Brinsupri as the main attraction, according to trade publication Fierce Pharma.

stories.headline: New York City and state sue to block federal rule on housing aid for mixed-status families
stories.summary: New York City and New York State joined a multistate lawsuit filed Monday against the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development over a rule on families in which some members lack eligible immigration status. The plaintiffs want a court to stop the rule before it takes effect next month.
stories.why_it_matters: Families in public housing or using federal rental vouchers that include a member without eligible immigration status could have to choose between living together and keeping their aid. Outlets on the left, center and right all reported the suit, the national ones through the same wire story.
stories.background: Federal law limits housing assistance to citizens and certain non-citizens, and until now a household with a mix of eligible and ineligible members could receive reduced, prorated aid covering only the eligible ones. HUD finalized a rule this month that changes how citizenship and immigration status are verified for everyone in federally assisted housing, according to Bloomberg Government. A coalition of state attorneys general, co-led by New York's Letitia James and California's Rob Bonta, formally opposed the proposal in a comment letter in April. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the city's participation in the lawsuit on Monday.

facts.text: A coalition of nearly two dozen plaintiffs, including New York City, sued the Trump administration on Monday to stop the rule from taking effect next month, THE CITY reported.
New York State is also a plaintiff, and state Attorney General Letitia James is among those suing HUD.

The rule would bar families with undocumented members from living in public housing or receiving certain rental vouchers, according to THE CITY; Gothamist describes it as stripping eligible citizens of assistance if any household member does not qualify because of immigration status.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Monday that the city had joined the federal lawsuit.

A separate lawsuit by Los Angeles nonprofit groups cites HUD figures putting about 79,300 people in mixed-status households that receive HUD assistance, including roughly 36,000 eligible children, Bloomberg Government reported.

In April, 22 attorneys general co-led by California's Rob Bonta and New York's Letitia James filed a comment letter opposing the proposed rule, arguing it would violate the Administrative Procedure Act.

stories.headline: New York's top court upholds ban on turning away Section 8 renters
stories.summary: The New York State Court of Appeals on Monday upheld the state law that bars landlords from discriminating against tenants who pay rent with federal housing vouchers. The court reversed lower-court rulings that had struck the protection down and dismissed a landlord's challenge.
stories.why_it_matters: New Yorkers who rely on Section 8 vouchers keep the legal right not to be rejected by a landlord because of how they pay rent. Coverage in the digest came from two left-leaning outlets and one right-leaning one.
stories.background: Section 8 is a federal program that pays part of the rent for low-income tenants in privately owned apartments. New York added 'source of income' protections to state law in 2019, making it illegal for landlords to refuse tenants because they use a voucher. In one earlier challenge, the state attorney general sued an Ithaca landlord, Jason Fane, in 2022, accusing him of refusing vouchers, and a mid-level appeals court, the Appellate Division's Third Department, later ruled the protections unconstitutional, reasoning that forcing landlords into the program exposed them to inspections of property and records they had not consented to. The Court of Appeals is the state's highest court. The summaries available for this brief do not name the case decided Monday.

facts.text: The Court of Appeals reversed lower-court rulings that had struck down state protections against Section 8 discrimination.
The court dismissed a landlord's challenge to the law prohibiting discrimination against renters who rely on federal housing vouchers, The New York Times reported.

In an earlier case that began with a 2022 suit by the attorney general against Ithaca landlord Jason Fane, the Appellate Division's Third Department held that the 2019 source-of-income protections violated landlords' Fourth Amendment rights.

stories.headline: City and Lyft agree to cap Citi Bike e-bike rides at $3.65 for members
stories.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Monday a deal with Lyft, which operates Citi Bike, to cap the price of an electric bike ride of up to 45 minutes at $3.65 for members. The cap starts in January, and membership prices are frozen through May 2029.
stories.why_it_matters: Annual members who take long e-bike trips would pay far less per ride; the change does not apply to riders without a membership.
stories.background: Citi Bike is New York's bike-share system, run by the ride-hailing company Lyft under a contract with the city. Members pay an annual fee and then a per-minute charge for electric bikes, and those charges have risen several times in recent years. The advocacy group Transportation Alternatives campaigned this year for a $3 cap on member e-bike rides under 45 minutes. Streetsblog reported in October that city transportation officials had said changes would have to wait until the contract comes up for renewal in 2029.

facts.text: The city reached an agreement with Lyft to cap a 45-minute electric Citi Bike ride at $3.65 for members, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Monday.
The cap begins in January and could save members as much as $8.50 per trip, Brooklyn Paper reported; The New York Times put the current high for such a ride at more than $12.
The agreement also freezes membership prices through May 2029.
The savings apply only to riders who already pay for an annual membership, which the New York Post put at $249.

stories.headline: Retired NYPD detective ordered jailed on murder charge in George Washington Bridge shooting
stories.summary: Victor Romero, a retired NYPD detective, was ordered held in jail Monday after being charged with second-degree murder in the killing of Koran Irvine on the George Washington Bridge last month. Romero has pleaded not guilty.
stories.why_it_matters: The case tests how prosecutors and courts treat a former police officer accused of killing another driver, and it has drawn organized public attention. Only left-leaning outlets in the digest covered Monday's hearing.
stories.background: Koran Irvine was shot and killed on the George Washington Bridge in October in what police described as a road-rage encounter. Police said surveillance video showed Irvine's car swerving into another lane and nearly colliding with a Range Rover driven by Romero. Romero, 62, left the NYPD about 25 years ago. He was first arraigned on a manslaughter charge and a judge set bail at $1 million, which Irvine's family objected to. A Manhattan grand jury later indicted him on second-degree murder.

facts.text: Romero was ordered held in jail; The New York Times reported he was charged with second-degree murder and held without bail.

Prosecutors said Romero scrubbed his car after the shooting, according to The New York Times.
Dozens of people, including activist Hawk Newsome, came to court in support of Irvine, Gothamist reported.
A Manhattan grand jury indicted Romero on second-degree murder, an upgrade from the manslaughter charge at his first arraignment, when bail was set at $1 million.

stories.headline: City report says yellow cab fare increases could keep drivers out of poverty
stories.summary: A city report found that raising yellow taxi fares could keep drivers out of poverty, Gothamist reported Tuesday. The Taxi and Limousine Commission has approved one fare increase for yellow cabs in the past 14 years.
stories.why_it_matters: If the city acts on the finding, cab rides would cost passengers more while drivers would earn more per trip. Gothamist is the only outlet in the digest reporting on it.
stories.background: The Taxi and Limousine Commission, a city agency, sets the metered fares that yellow cabs may charge. Its last increase came in 2022, when commissioners approved a rise of about 23 percent on average and lifted the base fare from $2.50 to $3. Unlike drivers for Uber and Lyft, yellow cab drivers have no minimum pay standard, a point their union raised at the time.

markets.summary: Monday's trading was dominated by one company: Nvidia shares closed about 31 percent higher after the chipmaker brought Jensen Huang back as chief executive, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose about 3 percent. That followed a sharp sell-off in artificial-intelligence stocks last week; the S&P 500 is still down about 11 percent over the past month. Tech shares in Asia and Europe rose on Tuesday, but US stock futures (bets on where indexes will open) pointed lower, with Nvidia slipping in premarket trading as lawmakers criticized the White House's role in Huang's return. Anthropic, the AI lab that went public recently, fell below its $83 offering price before the open. Separately, New York Fed President John Williams said inflation is still too high and that interest rates may need to go higher over time.

concept.explanation: US stock exchanges open at 9:30 a.m. Eastern, but shares can change hands electronically for several hours before that, in what is called premarket trading. Fewer people trade then, so prices can swing more on news such as earnings, a political fight or a change of chief executive, and the moves give an early hint of how a stock may open. It reaches your wallet through retirement and index funds: they are priced during regular hours, but a large premarket drop in a big company like Nvidia often carries into the opening price of the funds that hold it.
